description: Emma Bovary confuses real life with the romantic novels she has read. Flaubert invents the modern novel, and the trial that makes it famous.

hero.hook: A woman bored in the provinces. Then adultery, debt, and a word that would become a diagnosis.

blocks.text: In **1857**, **Gustave Flaubert** published **Madame Bovary**, the novel of a woman disappointed by provincial life who sinks into adultery. The book broke with everything before it. This is where **[[realism]]** begins: a movement that wants to describe life as it is, without making it beautiful.

Flaubert was put on trial for immorality. The case turned the novel into a scandal, then into a classic. Through **Emma Bovary**, he asks what fiction does to our lives. The book shows how dreams fed by reading can destroy the real.

**Gustave Flaubert** shut himself away at **Croisset**, near Rouen, and gave **five years**, from 1851 to 1856, to this novel. His rule was the “mot juste,” the exact word, no more and no less, with no repetition and no lyrical swelling. The writer must disappear: what counts is the style, not an author pushing himself forward.

blocks.caption: Flaubert: the craftsman of pure style

blocks.text: “Madame Bovary is me,” Flaubert said. He did not mean autobiography, but total immersion in his heroine's pain.

He hated cheap **romanticism**, the hollow kind full of clichés, while admitting the pull of the dream in himself. That tension feeds Emma's drama. Flaubert also wrote famous letters about his nights of work on a single sentence.

sections.title: Flaubert and the discipline of the right word

blocks.text: **Emma Rouault** grew up in a convent on sentimental novels, stories full of exalted passion. She marries **Charles Bovary**, an honest but dull country doctor. The couple settles in **Yonville-l'Abbaye**, a small Norman town where nothing looks like the heroines Emma has read about.

blocks.caption: The Norman countryside: the setting of the boredom that pushes Emma into adultery

blocks.text: To escape that boredom, Emma loves **Rodolphe Boulanger**, a landowner of the district, then **Léon Dupuis**, a lawyer's clerk. Each lover turns out to be as ordinary as her husband. The merchant **Lheureux** pushes her into debt, and her purchases on credit ruin her. The novel grew out of a news story, the **Delphine Delamare** case, a woman who died in **1848**.

Flaubert invents **[[Free indirect speech]]**. The technique blends the narrator's voice with the character's thoughts, with no quotation marks and no “she thought that.” The reader gets inside Emma's head and keeps an ironic distance at the same time. You can no longer always tell whether Emma or the narrator is speaking.

In **1857**, Flaubert was acquitted of “offense against public morals.” Emma kills herself with **arsenic** stolen from the pharmacist **[[Homais]]**, a figure of the triumphant, mediocre middle class. Charles dies of grief, their daughter **Berthe** goes to work in a factory, and Homais receives the Legion of Honor. There is no poetic justice: the world stays unfair.

sections.title: Free indirect speech and the trial

blocks.text: The philosopher **Jules de Gaultier** coined the term **[[Bovarysm]]**, the chronic dissatisfaction of someone who prefers the fantasy to the real. Emma is not only an adulterous wife. She is the first great figure of modern frustration, tied to consumption, to the hunger for objects, luxury and passion.

Flaubert puts form above subject: a book about “nothing,” the life of a bored woman, can be a masterpiece if the style is perfect. Every scene is built like a painting, with exact details that reveal Emma's inner emptiness. **Marcel Proust**, **Franz Kafka** and the **Nouveau Roman**, the 20th-century movement that broke narrative conventions, owe him a great deal. The 1857 trial also turned the novel into a matter of public debate.
**Madame Bovary**, published in **1857**, revolutionizes the novel through **[[Free indirect speech]]** and **[[Bovarysm]]**: mistaking the fictions you read for real life can end in disaster.
